title: Chapter 02: Git, GitHub & Markdown

sections.title: 1. Git Core: Repositories, Commits & The Three Areas
sections.description: Understand how Git stores snapshots instead of file-by-file diffs, why commit hashes make history tamper-evident, and how changes flow across the Three Areas.

blocks.title: Distributed Version Control: Repositories & Clones
blocks.content:
Before Git (created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for the Linux kernel), many teams used **centralized** version control systems where only a single server held the full project history. If the server went offline, you could not commit or inspect past versions.

Git is a **distributed version control system (DVCS)**:

* **Every clone is a complete repository:** When you run `git clone <url>`, you download the project files **and** the entire commit history. You can commit, create branches, and inspect `git log` completely offline.
* **Local vs. Remote (`origin`):** By convention, the shared copy hosted on GitHub is named `origin` (your **remote**), while the copy on your machine is your **local repository**.
* **CLI First:** Learning Git from the command line means your skills work identically on your laptop, inside a Docker container, or over SSH on a headless Linux server.

> [!NOTE]
> **Non-Example (The "Final_v2_REAL.zip" Trap):** Manually copying project folders (`project-v1`, `project-v2-fixed`) does not record *who* changed *what*, *why* they changed it, or how to cleanly combine two teammates' edits. Git replaces ad-hoc folder copies with an immutable, cryptographically linked history.

blocks.title: Commits, SHA Hashes & Tags
blocks.content:
A **commit** is not a list of line-by-line patches—it is a **snapshot** of the entire tracked project at a specific point in time, linked to its parent commit(s).

### Why Commit Hashes Make History Tamper-Evident
Every commit is identified by a unique cryptographic **SHA hash** (e.g., `2ea9f1c4d5ef42ee3cf1b0d3849a0445ad8d2683`), computed from:
1. The exact snapshot content (files and directories)
2. Its parent commit hash(es)
3. The author and committer metadata (name, email, timestamp)
4. The commit message

Because all four inputs feed into the hash, **commits are immutable**: if you change a single character in a file, parent, author, or message, Git does not edit the existing commit—it creates a **brand-new commit with a different hash**, leaving the old one behind. Commands like `git commit --amend` and `git rebase` actually create new commits rather than mutating old ones.

### Human-Friendly Labels: Tags & Signatures
* **Tags (`git tag v1.0.0`):** A tag attaches a memorable, fixed name to one specific commit—typically a software release or milestone submission.
* **Signed Commits:** Cryptographically signing a commit with your SSH key proves *who created the commit* (earning a **Verified** badge on GitHub), preventing anyone from spoofing your `user.name` and `user.email`.

blocks.title: The Three Areas: Working Directory, Staging Area & Repository
blocks.content:
Why doesn't Git save changes straight from your text editor into permanent history? Because while coding, you often edit three files at once—two for a new feature and one quick typo fix. You want to commit them as **two separate, logical snapshots**, not one messy bundle.

Git solves this with **three distinct areas** on your machine:

| Area | Role | Primary Commands |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Working Directory** | The actual files on your disk that you edit in your IDE/editor. | Edit files, `git diff` (shows unstaged changes) |
| **2. Staging Area (Index)** | A draft "loading dock" holding the exact changes queued for the *next* commit. | `git add <file>`, `git status` |
| **3. Local Repository (`.git`)** | The permanent, committed snapshot history stored locally. | `git commit -m "..."`, `git log` |

> [!TIP]
> **Diagnostic Reflex:** Whenever you feel lost in Git, run `git status`. It tells you which branch `HEAD` is on, which files are modified in the **working directory**, which are staged in the **index**, and whether your local branch is ahead of or behind `origin/main`.

blocks.title: Dataflow Across Git's Three Areas and Remote
blocks.caption: Changes move forward from Working Directory to Staging Area to Local Repository, and synchronize with the Remote via push/fetch/pull.

blocks.title: Annotated Git Command Cheat Sheet
blocks.code:
git clone git@github.com:org/repo.git   # Copy remote repo + full history
git status                              # Inspect working dir vs staging vs HEAD
git diff                                # Show unstaged line-by-line changes
git add README.md                       # Move changes into Staging Area
git commit -m "Add project README"      # Record permanent snapshot in Local Repo
git log                                 # View commit history (press q to quit)
git tag v1.0.0                          # Label the current commit as v1.0.0
git push                                # Upload local commits to origin

annotations.note: Always check `git status` before committing to verify no unintended files are staged.
`git add` stages a snapshot of the file as it exists *right now*. Further edits require another `git add`.
Commits only what is in the Staging Area—unstaged edits in the Working Directory remain untouched.

blocks.title: Simulate Git's Three Areas (Working -> Staging -> Commit)
blocks.instructions:
Complete `git_add(repo, filename)` and `git_commit(repo, message)` to model how Git moves file snapshots from `working` to `staging` and into `commits`.
- `git_add` should copy `repo['working'][filename]` into `repo['staging'][filename]`.
- `git_commit` should append a dictionary `{'message': message, 'snapshot': dict(repo['staging'])}` to `repo['commits']`.
Run the code to verify that unstaged edits after `git_add` do NOT sneak into the commit!
blocks.starter_code:
repo = {
    'working': {'README.md': 'v1'},
    'staging': {},
    'commits': []
}

def git_add(r, filename):
    # TODO: copy the file content from working to staging
    pass

def git_commit(r, message):
    # TODO: append {'message': message, 'snapshot': dict(r['staging'])} to r['commits']
    pass

git_add(repo, 'README.md')
repo['working']['README.md'] = 'v2-draft'  # Edited AFTER git add!
git_commit(repo, 'Add README v1')

print('Committed:', repo['commits'][0]['snapshot']['README.md'])
print('Working:', repo['working']['README.md'])
blocks.solution:
repo = {
    'working': {'README.md': 'v1'},
    'staging': {},
    'commits': []
}

def git_add(r, filename):
    r['staging'][filename] = r['working'][filename]

def git_commit(r, message):
    r['commits'].append({'message': message, 'snapshot': dict(r['staging'])})

git_add(repo, 'README.md')
repo['working']['README.md'] = 'v2-draft'  # Edited AFTER git add!
git_commit(repo, 'Add README v1')

print('Committed:', repo['commits'][0]['snapshot']['README.md'])
print('Working:', repo['working']['README.md'])
hints: In `git_add`, assign `r['staging'][filename] = r['working'][filename]`.
In `git_commit`, use `r['commits'].append({'message': message, 'snapshot': dict(r['staging'])})` so the commit stores an independent copy of the staged snapshot.

sections.title: 2. Branches, Merging, Rebasing & Resolving Conflicts
sections.description: See why branches are lightweight pointers, compare Merge vs. Rebase vs. Squash, and learn to resolve merge conflicts cleanly.

blocks.title: Branches & HEAD: Just Movable Pointers
blocks.content:
A common misconception is that creating a Git branch duplicates your entire project folder. In reality, **a branch is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to a single commit** (a tiny 41-byte file containing a 40-character SHA hash plus a newline).

* **`main`:** The conventional name for the primary, stable branch.
* **`HEAD`:** A special pointer indicating **where you currently are** (usually pointing to a branch name like `HEAD -> main`, which in turn points to a commit).
* **Why branching is instantaneous:** Running `git checkout -b feature-login` creates a new pointer at the current commit and moves `HEAD` to it. As you make commits on `feature-login`, `feature-login` advances automatically while `main` stays safely behind.

> [!NOTE]
> **Reading `git log`:**
> * `commit 2ea9f1c... (HEAD -> main)` means your local `main` is on `2ea9f1c` and you are currently checked out on `main`.
> * `commit 20f8741... (origin/main, origin/HEAD)` means the remote server is still one commit behind at `20f8741`.

blocks.title: Integrating Branches: Merge vs. Rebase vs. Squash
blocks.content:
Once your feature branch is ready, you bring its work back into `main` using one of three strategies:

| Strategy | How It Works | Resulting History | Best Used When |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Merge (Default)** | Combines both branches. If `main` has moved, creates a **3-way merge commit** with two parents; if `main` has not moved, performs a **fast-forward** (simply slides the `main` pointer forward). | Preserves exact branching topology and timestamps. | Merging Pull Requests in team repositories so everyone sees what entered `main`. |
| **Rebase** | Replays your branch's commits one by one on top of the latest `main`, generating **new commit hashes**. | Perfectly linear history with no merge commits. | Updating your local unpushed branch or cleaning up before pushing (`git pull --rebase`). |
| **Squash** | Collapses all commits on the feature branch into a **single commit** before merging into `main`. | One clean commit per feature on `main`. | Feature branches with lots of noisy `"WIP"` or `"fix typo"` commits. |

> [!WARNING]
> **Golden Rule of Rebasing:** Never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch that teammates are using! Because rebase rewrites commit hashes, teammates' histories will diverge from yours.

blocks.title: Commit DAG: 3-Way Merge vs. Linear Rebase
blocks.caption: A 3-way merge joins two diverged branches with a two-parent merge commit (M). Rebase replays feature commits (F1', F2') linearly on top of C2.

blocks.title: Merge Conflicts & Conflict Markers
blocks.content:
Git automatically merges changes when two branches edit different files—or even different lines of the same file. However, when two branches edit the **same lines** of the same file (or one deletes/renames a file the other modified), Git pauses the merge and asks a human to decide.

Git marks the disputed region directly inside the file using three markers:

1. `<<<<<<< HEAD`: Start of **your** current branch's version.
2. `=======`: Divider between the two conflicting versions.
3. `>>>>>>> other-branch`: End of the **incoming** branch's version.

### The 4-Step Conflict Resolution Ritual
1. Open the conflicted file in your editor.
2. Decide what the final text should be (keep `HEAD`, keep `other-branch`, or combine both) and **delete all three marker lines** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`).
3. Stage the resolved file: `git add <file>`.
4. Conclude the operation: `git commit` (for a merge) or `git rebase --continue` (for a rebase).

blocks.title: Anatomy of a Git Merge Conflict
blocks.code:
# Project Title

<<<<<<< HEAD
Built for HEIG-VD DAI (2026) using Java 21.
=======
Built for HEIG-VD DAI using Java 21 and Docker.
>>>>>>> feature-docker

## Installation

annotations.note: Start marker: everything between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is what exists on your current branch.
Separator between the two competing versions.
End marker: everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feature-docker` comes from the incoming branch. Delete all 3 markers when resolving!

blocks.title: Parse & Resolve Git Conflict Markers
blocks.instructions:
Implement `resolveConflict(text, strategy)` to parse a conflicted file containing `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>> feature` markers.
- Extract `ours` (lines between `<<<<<<<` and `=======`) and `theirs` (lines between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`).
- If `strategy === 'ours'`, return `ours`; if `'theirs'`, return `theirs`; if `'both'`, return `ours + '\n' + theirs`.
Ensure no conflict markers remain in the output!
blocks.expected_output:
OURS: Port: 8080
THEIRS: Port: 9090
BOTH: Port: 8080
Port: 9090
hints: Use `lines.findIndex(l => l.startsWith('<<<<<<<'))` (and similarly for `=======` and `>>>>>>>`) to locate the three marker lines.
Slice between `start + 1` and `mid` for `ours`, and between `mid + 1` and `end` for `theirs`.

sections.title: 3. Repository Hygiene: .gitignore Patterns & Negation
sections.description: Keep build artifacts, IDE settings, and secrets out of Git history using .gitignore rules, root anchoring, and negation (!).

blocks.title: What Belongs in Git (and What Does Not)
blocks.content:
A `.gitignore` file at the root of your repository tells Git which untracked files to ignore so they never clutter `git status` or accidentally get committed.

### The Golden Rule of Repository Hygiene
> **Commit what a human wrote or chose; never commit what the build produces.**

| Commit (Track in Git) | Ignore (Add to `.gitignore`) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Source code (`.java`, `.py`, `.js`), `pom.xml`, `Dockerfile` | Build outputs (`target/`, `dist/`, `*.class`, `*.jar`) |
| Documentation (`README.md`) & small README images | IDE config (`.idea/`, `.vscode/`, `*.iml`) |
| Small example/input files needed to run demos | Secrets & credentials (`.env`, private SSH keys, API tokens) |

### Pattern Syntax & Negation (`!`)
* `*.txt` — matches any `.txt` file at any depth.
* `/target/` — the leading slash anchors the pattern to the **repository root** only (so `src/target/` would not be ignored), and the trailing slash matches directories.
* `!examples/**/*_input.txt` — the leading `!` **negates** a previous ignore rule, re-including matching files as exceptions.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Already-Tracked Files:** `.gitignore` only prevents *untracked* files from being staged. If a file was already committed before you added it to `.gitignore`, Git will keep tracking it until you remove it from the index with `git rm --cached <file>`.

blocks.title: Annotated .gitignore Example
blocks.code:
# Ignore all text files...
*.txt

# ...except the input files of the examples
!examples/**/*_input.txt

# Ignore the target directory at the root only
/target/

# IDE and OS clutter
.idea/
.DS_Store

annotations.note: Wildcard extension match: ignores every `.txt` file anywhere in the repo.
Negation (`!`): overrides line 2 for files ending in `_input.txt` inside `examples/`.
Leading `/` anchors to repo root; trailing `/` ensures it only matches a directory named `target`.

blocks.title: Evaluate .gitignore Patterns with Negation (!)
blocks.instructions:
Implement `is_ignored(path, rules)` where `rules` are evaluated top-to-bottom (last matching rule wins):
- Ignore blank lines or lines starting with `#`.
- If a rule starts with `!`, it is a negation (`negated = True`, strip `!`).
- Support `*.ext` (matches `path.endswith(ext)`), `/dir/` (matches `path.startswith(dir + '/')`), and `fnmatch` glob patterns.
Test your function against `notes.txt`, `examples/lab1_input.txt`, `target/App.class`, and `src/Main.java`.
blocks.starter_code:
import fnmatch

rules = [
    '# Ignore all text files',
    '*.txt',
    '!examples/*_input.txt',
    '/target/'
]

def is_ignored(path, rules):
    ignored = False
    for raw in rules:
        rule = raw.strip()
        if not rule or rule.startswith('#'):
            continue
        # TODO: handle '!' negation, '/dir/' root-anchored dirs, and fnmatch patterns
    return ignored

files = ['notes.txt', 'examples/lab1_input.txt', 'target/App.class', 'src/Main.java']
for f in files:
    print(f'{f}: {"IGNORED" if is_ignored(f, rules) else "TRACKED"}')
blocks.expected_output:
notes.txt: IGNORED
examples/lab1_input.txt: TRACKED
target/App.class: IGNORED
src/Main.java: TRACKED
hints: Check `negated = rule.startswith('!')` and strip the `!` before matching.
When a rule matches, set `ignored = not negated` so later `!` rules can un-ignore a file.

sections.title: 4. GitHub, SSH Authentication & Team Workflows
sections.description: Configure passwordless SSH authentication and commit signing, collaborate via Issues and Pull Requests, and recover from rejected pushes.

blocks.title: GitHub Collaboration: Users, Orgs, Issues, PRs & Forks
blocks.content:
While **Git** is the distributed version control tool running on your machine, **GitHub** is the cloud platform hosting your remote repositories and adding social collaboration tools on top:

* **Users vs. Organizations:** A repository belongs either to a personal user account (e.g., your profile README repo `<username>/<username>`) or to an **Organization** shared by a team (such as your DAI practical work team).
* **Issues:** Track bugs, tasks, and feature ideas with assignees, labels, and discussion threads. Opening an issue *before* coding prevents duplicated or unwanted work.
* **Pull Requests (PRs):** Propose merging commits from a feature branch into `main`. Teammates review the diff, leave line-by-line comments, request changes, or approve before merging.
* **Forks:** Your own server-side copy of *someone else's* repository—the standard way to contribute to open-source projects where you do not have direct write access.

blocks.title: SSH Authentication & Signed Commits (Verified Badge)
blocks.content:
Typing passwords on every `git push` is tedious and insecure. Instead, you authenticate using an **SSH key pair** (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519` and `id_ed25519.pub`):

* **Authentication Key:** You upload the **public key** (`.pub`) to GitHub under *SSH keys (Authentication)*. Your **private key** never leaves your machine! Testing with `ssh -T git@github.com` replies `Hi <username>! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.` (a non-zero exit code is normal here).
* **Signing Key (Git >= 2.34):** Anyone can configure `git config user.name "Linus Torvalds"`. To prove *you* actually created a commit, you add the same `.pub` key to GitHub as a **Signing key** and enable SSH signing:

```bash
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgSign true
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **What the "Verified" Badge Proves (and What It Doesn't):**
> A GitHub **Verified** badge cryptographically proves that the commit was signed by the holder of that registered SSH key. It proves **who made the commit**—it does *not* prove who originally wrote the code inside it (for example, if you copy-pasted code from a teammate or AI).

blocks.title: Team Workflows: Pull-Request Workflow vs. Centralized Workflow
blocks.content:
When your whole team has write access to a shared repository, two workflows exist:

### 1. Pull-Request Workflow (Recommended)
1. Open an **Issue** describing the task.
2. Create a **feature branch** off `main` (`git checkout -b fix-port-parsing`).
3. Commit and push to the branch (`git push -u origin fix-port-parsing`).
4. Open a **Pull Request** (use a *Draft PR* if it is not ready for review yet).
5. A teammate (not the author) reviews the diff and merges the PR.
6. Delete the remote branch, then locally run `git checkout main`, `git pull`, and `git branch -d fix-port-parsing`.

### 2. Centralized Workflow & The Rejected Push
If teammates push directly to `main` (or two PRs merge into `main` back-to-back), you will eventually hit:

```text
! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/...'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally.
```

Nothing is broken—a teammate pushed to `main` before you. Configure Git once with `git config --global pull.rebase true`, then run `git pull` (replaying your local commits on top of theirs) and `git push`. If a conflict occurs during `git pull`, resolve the markers, run `git add <file>`, `git rebase --continue`, and `git push`.

blocks.title: Recommended Team Pull-Request Workflow
blocks.caption: End-to-end collaboration cycle: Issue -> Branch -> Push -> Peer Review -> Merge -> Local Sync.
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor Dev as Developer
  participant Git as Local Repo
  participant GH as GitHub (origin)
  actor Rev as Teammate (Reviewer)

  Dev->>GH: Open Issue describing task
  Dev->>Git: git checkout -b feat-login
  Dev->>Git: git add & git commit (signed)
  Dev->>GH: git push -u origin feat-login
  Dev->>GH: Open Pull Request
  Rev->>GH: Review diff & Approve
  Rev->>GH: Merge PR into main & delete branch
  Dev->>Git: git checkout main && git pull
  Dev->>Git: git branch -d feat-login

blocks.caption: Decision flow when `git push` is rejected because `origin/main` has newer commits.

sections.title: 5. Documentation as Code: Markdown & GFM
sections.description: Write clean, diffable, portable technical documentation in CommonMark and GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM).

blocks.title: Why Markdown? Diffable, Portable & GFM
blocks.content:
Code is only half of your deliverable—the other half (READMEs, protocol specs, PW reports) is written in **Markdown** (created by John Gruber and Aaron Swartz in 2004). Why use Markdown instead of `.docx` inside a Git repository? 1. **Diffable:** Because Markdown is plain text, `git diff` shows the exact sentence you changed. A `.docx` file is a binary ZIP archive—Git cannot show meaningful line diffs or merge two teammates' edits. 2. **Portable:** The same `.md` file renders natively on GitHub, converts to HTML/PDF/slides via Pandoc or Quarto, and remains readable in any plain-text editor. ### CommonMark vs. GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) * **CommonMark:** The strict, unambiguous baseline specification. * **GFM:** CommonMark *plus* **tables**, **task lists** (`- [ ]`), **strikethrough** (`~~text~~`), and **autolinks**—the dialect GitHub renders in READMEs, Issues, and PRs. ### Two Classic Pitfalls to Avoid 1. **Missing blank lines:** A blank line separates blocks. A list glued immediately below a paragraph with no blank line may fail to render as a list. 2. **Single line breaks in `.md` files vs. GitHub Issues:** In `.md` files, a single newline inside a paragraph is ignored (so wrapping at 80 chars still renders as one paragraph). In GitHub Issues/PRs, however, GitHub turns every newline into a visible `
` line break.

blocks.title: Annotated Markdown & GFM Reference
blocks.code:
# Project Title
## Features

**Bold**, _italic_, ~~deprecated~~, and `inline code`.

- [x] Configure SSH signing
- [ ] Open first Pull Request

| Command | Purpose |
| ------- | ------: |
| `git status` | Inspect state |

```java
System.out.println("Hello, DAI!");
```

annotations.note: GFM task list syntax (`- [x]` checked, `- [ ]` unchecked) — renders interactive checkboxes in GitHub Issues and PRs.
GFM table: `------:` right-aligns the second column.
Always specify the language (`java`, `bash`, `python`) after the opening triple backticks for syntax highlighting.

blocks.title: Build a Mini Markdown / GFM Linter
blocks.instructions:
Write `lint_markdown(md)` to catch two common Markdown mistakes from Chapter 02:
1. **Bare code fence:** An opening ` ``` ` line with no language tag (e.g., `line.strip() == '```'` when not currently inside a code block).
2. **Glued list:** A list item (`- ` or `* `) immediately following a non-empty non-list line without a blank line in between.
Print each warning found.

Here are the steps:
- Step 1
- Step 2

```

```
"""

def lint_markdown(md):
    warnings = []
    lines = md.splitlines()
    in_code = False
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        stripped = line.strip()
        # TODO: toggle in_code on ``` and warn if opening fence has no language
        # TODO: warn if not in_code, line starts with '- ', and previous line is non-empty text (not a list)
    return warnings

for w in lint_markdown(sample_md):

blocks.expected_output:
Line 3: Missing blank line before list
Line 6: Code fence missing language tag
blocks.solution:
sample_md = """# Report
Here are the steps:
- Step 1
- Step 2

```
echo hello
```
"""

def lint_markdown(md):
    warnings = []
    lines = md.splitlines()
    in_code = False
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        stripped = line.strip()
        if stripped.startswith('```'):
            if not in_code and stripped == '```':
                warnings.append(f'Line {i + 1}: Code fence missing language tag')
            in_code = not in_code
            continue
        if not in_code and stripped.startswith('- ') and i > 0:
            prev = lines[i - 1].strip()
            if prev and not prev.startswith('- '):
                warnings.append(f'Line {i + 1}: Missing blank line before list')
    return warnings

for w in lint_markdown(sample_md):
    print(w)
hints: Track `in_code = not in_code` whenever `stripped.startswith('```')`. Before flipping `in_code`, if `not in_code and stripped == '```'`, record a missing-language warning.
For glued lists, check `not in_code and stripped.startswith('- ') and i > 0` and verify `lines[i - 1].strip()` is non-empty and does not start with `'- '`.

sections.title: 6. Synthesis, Diagnostic Quiz & Spaced Repetition
sections.description: Articulate the Git mental model in plain language, test your diagnostic reflexes on real scenarios, and lock in key concepts with flashcards.

blocks.concept: Git's Snapshot Model, Commit Hashes & Branches
blocks.target_audience: a first-year CS student who thinks Git works like Google Docs Track Changes
blocks.prompt: Explain why Git is not just a folder-backup or 'Track Changes' diff tool. Cover: (1) why a commit is a snapshot with a tamper-evident hash, (2) why creating a branch is instantaneous, and (3) why the Staging Area exists between your editor and the repository.
key_points_to_cover: Commits are project snapshots linked to parent hashes (immutable)
Changing anything produces a new commit hash rather than mutating the old one
Branches are tiny movable pointers to a commit, not folder copies
Staging Area lets you craft clean, logical commits from messy working-directory edits

blocks.title: Synthesis: Team Collaboration, Rejected Pushes & Commit Verification
blocks.prompt: Your teammate pushed commits directly to `main`, and now your `git push` is rejected. Explain: (1) why it happened, (2) how `git pull --rebase` resolves it (including if a conflict occurs), and (3) what GitHub's 'Verified' badge guarantees—and does not guarantee—about your commits.
self_check_criteria: Explained that `origin/main` advanced ahead of local `main`, so Git refuses a non-fast-forward push to prevent overwriting teammate work.
Described `git pull --rebase` (replaying local commits on top of remote commits) and the conflict loop (`edit markers -> git add -> git rebase --continue -> git push`).
Distinguished that the Verified badge proves who signed/created the commit with a registered key, NOT who originally authored the code inside it.
blocks.model_answer: A rejected push (`fetch first`) happens because `origin/main` contains commits your local repository does not have yet; pushing directly would overwrite them. Running `git pull` with `pull.rebase = true` fetches the remote commits and replays your local commits on top of them. If both touched the same lines, Git pauses at the conflict: you remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers, run `git add <file>`, `git rebase --continue`, and finally `git push`. Meanwhile, GitHub's Verified badge cryptographically proves that the commit was signed by the holder of the registered SSH signing key (preventing `user.name`/`user.email` spoofing), but it does not prove who originally wrote the code.

blocks.title: The Three Areas: Staging vs. Working Directory
blocks.question: You edit `App.java`, run `git add App.java`, and then make one more edit to `App.java` **without** running `git add` again. Next, you run `git commit -m "Update App"`. What gets committed?
options: Only the version of `App.java` from the moment you ran `git add App.java`.
The latest version of `App.java` currently saved on disk in the working directory.
Nothing—Git aborts the commit because `App.java` has unstaged modifications.
Both versions are committed as two separate commits automatically.
blocks.correct_answer: Only the version of `App.java` from the moment you ran `git add App.java`.
blocks.explanation:
`git commit` always records a snapshot of the **Staging Area (Index)**, not the Working Directory. When you ran `git add App.java`, Git copied the file's content at that moment into the Staging Area. Your subsequent edit only modified the Working Directory.

* 'The latest version on disk' confuses the Working Directory with the Staging Area.
* 'Git aborts the commit' is false—Git happily commits what is staged while leaving the newer edit unstaged (`Changes not staged for commit`).
* 'Two separate commits' never happens automatically.
hints: Recall the three areas: Working Directory, Staging Area, and Local Repository.
Which area does `git commit` actually read from?

blocks.title: Commit Hash Immutability
blocks.question: You run `git commit --amend -m "Fix typo in message"` to change only the commit message of your latest commit (without changing any files). What happens to the commit's SHA hash?
options: Git creates a brand-new commit with a different SHA hash, leaving the old commit behind.
Git edits the message in place and keeps the exact same SHA hash because no files changed.
Git keeps the same SHA hash unless you also ran `git add`.
Git appends `-amended` to the existing SHA hash.
blocks.correct_answer: Git creates a brand-new commit with a different SHA hash, leaving the old commit behind.
blocks.explanation:
A commit's SHA hash is computed from its content, parent(s), author/committer metadata, **and** commit message. Changing any of these inputs produces a completely different hash. Therefore, `git commit --amend` creates a new commit object and moves the branch pointer to it.

* Editing in place with the same hash is impossible in Git's content-addressed model.
* File changes are not required to change the hash—message changes alone change it.
* SHA hashes are fixed-length hexadecimal digests, never suffixed with `-amended`.
hints: List the four inputs used to compute a Git commit's SHA hash.
If one of those inputs changes, can the cryptographic hash stay the same?

blocks.title: What a Branch Is, Physically
blocks.question: Physically, a Git branch is not a copy of your project directory; it is simply a lightweight, movable ___ to a single commit.
blocks.explanation: In Git, a branch is just a movable **pointer** (a tiny file storing a 40-character commit SHA hash). That is why creating or switching branches is instantaneous regardless of project size.
hints: Think about why `git checkout -b feature` takes milliseconds even on a massive repository like the Linux kernel.
The word also describes `HEAD`.

blocks.title: Comparing Merge, Rebase & Squash
blocks.question: Which of the following statements about `merge`, `rebase`, and `squash` are accurate? (Select all that apply)
options: A 3-way merge creates a new merge commit with two parent commits.
Rebasing replays your branch's commits onto the target branch, creating a linear history with new commit hashes.
Squashing collapses all commits from a feature branch into a single commit before merging.
Rebasing commits that have already been pushed to a shared team branch is safe and recommended.
correct_answer: A 3-way merge creates a new merge commit with two parent commits.
Rebasing replays your branch's commits onto the target branch, creating a linear history with new commit hashes.
Squashing collapses all commits from a feature branch into a single commit before merging.
blocks.explanation: 3-way merges tie two diverged histories together via a two-parent merge commit. Rebasing replays commits on top of another base, producing a linear history with brand-new SHA hashes. Squashing condenses noisy feature-branch commits into one clean commit. However, **rebasing already-pushed shared commits is dangerous** because rewriting hashes causes teammates' local histories to diverge.
hints: Check each strategy's effect on commit hashes and parent pointers.
Remember the Golden Rule of Rebasing regarding shared branches.

blocks.title: Reading Merge Conflict Markers
blocks.question:
You are on branch `main` and run `git merge feature-timeout`. Git reports a conflict in `config.txt`:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 30
=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> feature-timeout
```

If you want to keep `feature-timeout`'s value and properly resolve the conflict, what should `config.txt` contain before you run `git add config.txt`?
options: timeout = 60
timeout = 30

=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> feature-timeout

<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> feature-timeout
blocks.explanation:
In a conflict block, `<<<<<<< HEAD` through `=======` shows your current branch (`main`), while `=======` through `>>>>>>> feature-timeout` shows the incoming branch (`feature-timeout`). To resolve the conflict, you keep the desired line (`timeout = 60`) and **delete all three conflict marker lines** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`).

* `timeout = 30` keeps `HEAD` instead of `feature-timeout`.
* The other two options leave Git's conflict markers in the file, which breaks configuration parsing.
hints: Which section represents the incoming `feature-timeout` branch: above or below `=======`?
What must you always do with the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` lines?

blocks.title: Evaluating .gitignore Rules & Negation
blocks.question:
Given this `.gitignore`:

```gitignore
*.txt
!examples/**/*_input.txt
/target/
```

Which file will **NOT** be ignored (i.e., will remain trackable by Git)?
options: examples/lab1/demo_input.txt
notes.txt
target/classes/Main.class
examples/lab1/readme.txt
blocks.explanation:
Rule 1 (`*.txt`) initially ignores all `.txt` files. Rule 2 (`!examples/**/*_input.txt`) negates that rule for any file ending in `_input.txt` under `examples/`, so `examples/lab1/demo_input.txt` is tracked.

* `notes.txt` matches `*.txt` and is not rescued by `!`.
* `target/classes/Main.class` is inside `/target/` at the repo root, so it is ignored.
* `examples/lab1/readme.txt` does not end with `_input.txt`, so it stays ignored.
hints: Remember that `.gitignore` rules are evaluated top-to-bottom, and `!` negates a previous match.
Check the exact filename suffix required by `!examples/**/*_input.txt`.

blocks.title: Diagnosing a Rejected Push
blocks.question: You run `git push` on `main` and see `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)`. What is the recommended recovery sequence if `pull.rebase` is set to `true`?
options: Run `git pull` to replay your commits on top of the remote's, resolve any conflicts if they occur, then run `git push`.
Run `git push --force` to overwrite the remote `main` with your local commits.
Delete your local repository and re-clone from GitHub.
Run `git commit --amend` and immediately try `git push` again.
blocks.correct_answer: Run `git pull` to replay your commits on top of the remote's, resolve any conflicts if they occur, then run `git push`.
blocks.explanation:
A rejected push means `origin/main` has commits you don't have locally yet (e.g., a teammate pushed before you). With `pull.rebase = true`, `git pull` fetches the remote commits and replays your local commits cleanly on top of them, after which `git push` succeeds.

* `git push --force` destroys your teammate's commits on the remote!
* Re-cloning discards or complicates your local unpushed work unnecessarily.
* `git commit --amend` only changes your local commit hash; it does not fetch the missing remote commits.
hints: Why did Git reject the push? Look at the hint: `(fetch first)`.
How do you integrate your teammate's commits before pushing yours?

blocks.title: What the GitHub Verified Badge Proves
blocks.question: Your teammate's commit on GitHub displays a green **Verified** badge. What does this badge cryptographically prove?
options: The commit was created by the holder of the SSH/GPG signing key registered to that GitHub account.
The code inside the commit has been unit-tested and contains no bugs.
Every line of code in the commit was typed personally by that teammate without AI or copy-paste.
The commit was pushed over HTTPS rather than SSH.
blocks.correct_answer: The commit was created by the holder of the SSH/GPG signing key registered to that GitHub account.
blocks.explanation:
Commit signing proves **who created the commit** by verifying a cryptographic signature against a public signing key registered on the user's GitHub account. This prevents `user.name` / `user.email` impersonation.

* It says nothing about code quality or tests (that's CI/CD's job).
* It cannot verify how the code inside the files was authored.
* SSH commit signing (`gpg.format = ssh`) works regardless of whether you push via SSH or HTTPS.
hints: Distinguish between *who created the Git commit* and *how the code was written or tested*.
What can someone spoof if commits are *not* signed?

blocks.title: Why Markdown Beats .docx in Git
blocks.question: Why is Markdown a much better fit than a Word (`.docx`) document inside a Git repository? (Select all that apply)
options: Markdown is plain text, so `git diff` shows exact line-by-line sentence changes.
Teammates can cleanly merge concurrent edits to different sections of a Markdown file.
Markdown is portable: the same source renders on GitHub and converts to PDF/HTML via tools like Pandoc.
Markdown automatically compiles Java code embedded inside fenced code blocks.
correct_answer: Markdown is plain text, so `git diff` shows exact line-by-line sentence changes.
Teammates can cleanly merge concurrent edits to different sections of a Markdown file.
Markdown is portable: the same source renders on GitHub and converts to PDF/HTML via tools like Pandoc.
blocks.explanation: Because Markdown is plain text, it is **diffable** (Git shows exact changed lines and can merge non-overlapping edits) and **portable** (readable anywhere, rendered by GitHub, and convertible to PDF/HTML/DOCX). Fenced code blocks (` ```java `) provide syntax highlighting for readers, not automatic compilation.
hints: Recall the two core properties highlighted in the chapter: *diffable* and *portable*.
Does Markdown execute or compile code blocks?

blocks.title: Standard Team Pull-Request Cycle
blocks.question: In the recommended team Pull-Request workflow, who should review and merge a Pull Request?
options: A teammate other than the PR author.
The PR author immediately after pushing, without waiting for anyone else.
GitHub's automated bot before any human reads the diff.
Only the course professor.
blocks.correct_answer: A teammate other than the PR author.
blocks.explanation:
In a team Pull-Request workflow, **a teammate (not the author)** reviews the diff, leaves feedback or approves, and merges the PR. This catches bugs early, spreads knowledge across the team, and keeps `main` clean.

* Self-merging without review defeats the purpose of a PR.
* Bots cannot judge architectural or logic correctness on their own.
hints: Think about why Pull Requests exist in a team of developers.
Who catches blind spots best—the author who just wrote the code, or a fresh pair of eyes?

blocks.title: Git's Three Areas
blocks.front: Name the **Three Areas** in Git between your editor and permanent history, and the command that moves changes between each.
blocks.back:
1. **Working Directory** (files on disk you edit) — inspect with `git diff`
2. **Staging Area / Index** (draft for next commit) — stage with `git add <file>`
3. **Local Repository** (`.git` committed history) — record with `git commit -m "..."`

blocks.title: Branch vs. HEAD
blocks.front: What is a **branch** in Git physically, and what is **`HEAD`**?
blocks.back:
* A **branch** is a lightweight, movable pointer to a single commit (a 40-char SHA hash).
* **`HEAD`** is a special pointer indicating where you currently are (normally pointing to the active branch, e.g., `HEAD -> main`).
blocks.hint: Neither one is a copy of your folder.

blocks.title: Commit Hash Immutability
blocks.front: What four things determine a Git commit's **SHA hash**, and why does `git commit --amend` change the hash?
blocks.back: A commit hash is computed from its **content**, **parent(s)**, **author/committer**, and **message**. Changing any of them creates a **new commit with a new hash**, leaving the old one behind.
blocks.hint: Content-addressed snapshots cannot be edited in place.

blocks.title: Merge vs. Rebase vs. Squash
blocks.front: Compare **Merge**, **Rebase**, and **Squash** when integrating a feature branch into `main`.
blocks.back:
* **Merge:** Combines both branches (creating a 2-parent merge commit if diverged, or fast-forwarding if not).
* **Rebase:** Replays your commits on top of the target branch (linear history, new hashes).
* **Squash:** Collapses all feature commits into a single commit before merging.

blocks.title: Conflict Markers & Resolution
blocks.front: What do `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>> branch` mean, and what are the steps to resolve a conflict?
blocks.back:
* Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======`: your current branch's version.
* Between `=======` and `>>>>>>> branch`: incoming branch's version.
* **Fix:** Edit the file to keep what stays, **delete all 3 marker lines**, then `git add <file>` and `git commit` (or `git rebase --continue`).

blocks.title: .gitignore Root & Negation
blocks.front: In `.gitignore`, what do a leading `/` (e.g., `/target/`) and a leading `!` (e.g., `!examples/*_input.txt`) mean?
blocks.back:
* Leading `/` anchors the match to the **repository root only**.
* Leading `!` **negates** a previous ignore pattern, re-including matching files as exceptions.

blocks.title: SSH Auth vs. Commit Signing
blocks.front: What is the difference between adding your SSH `.pub` key to GitHub as an **Authentication key** vs. a **Signing key**?
blocks.back:
* **Authentication key:** Lets you `git push`/`git pull` without typing passwords (`ssh -T git@github.com`).
* **Signing key:** Signs commits (`commit.gpgSign = true`, Git >= 2.34) so GitHub displays the **Verified** badge proving *who created the commit*.
blocks.hint: Transport authentication vs. commit authorship proof.

blocks.title: Recovering from a Rejected Push
blocks.front: Why does `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)` happen, and what is the recovery sequence?
blocks.back:
A teammate pushed commits to `origin/main` before you. With `git config --global pull.rebase true`, run:
1. `git pull` (replays your commits on top of theirs)
2. If a conflict occurs: resolve markers, `git add <file>`, `git rebase --continue`
3. `git push`
blocks.hint: Fetch and replay your commits on top of the remote's.

blocks.title: Fork vs. Branch on GitHub
blocks.front: When do you use a **branch** vs. a **fork** to contribute on GitHub?
blocks.back:
* **Branch:** When you have **write access** to the repository (e.g., your PW team repo).
* **Fork:** Your own copy of someone else's repo, used when you have **no write access** (e.g., open-source contributions).
blocks.hint: Write access vs. no write access.

blocks.title: GFM & Markdown Pitfalls
blocks.front: What does **GFM** add to CommonMark, and what are the two common newline/spacing pitfalls?
blocks.back:
* **GFM adds:** Tables, task lists (`- [ ]`), strikethrough (`~~`), and autolinks.
* **Pitfall 1:** Always leave a **blank line** before a list or block.
* **Pitfall 2:** Single newlines are ignored in `.md` files, but GitHub turns every newline into a visible line break in Issues/PRs.
blocks.hint: Tables + task lists; blank lines + single newlines.
